saint_pick.name: Vergilius of Salzburg
saint_pick.selection_reason: Vergilius of Salzburg died on 27 November 784, so his feast falls on the day, and he is well documented and unusual: an Irish monk-scholar called 'the Geometer', who built Salzburg's cathedral, evangelized Carinthia, and was denounced to the pope by Boniface for teaching that there were 'another world' and antipodes, yet was vindicated and canonized in 1233.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Canonized by Pope Gregory IX in 1233; commemorated on 27 November in the Roman Martyrology; patron saint of Salzburg and Carinthia (Austria), and venerated in Ireland.

beats.text: He was reported to the pope for believing in people beneath the earth.
beats.scene: A tonsured monk in a plain habit holds a round sphere in his hands at a table in a stone monastery room in eighth-century Bavaria. Through an arched window, a rider carries a sealed letter along the road toward distant Rome.

beats.text: Virgil was an Irish monk of the eighth century, later bishop of Salzburg, Austria.
He left Ireland meaning to visit the Holy Land, but settled among the Franks instead. Pippin welcomed him.
beats.scene: Pippin sits in an eighth-century Frankish hall of timber and stone, in a fur-trimmed tunic and cloak, welcoming a travel-worn Irish monk in a rough habit who holds a pilgrim's staff.

beats.text: Pippin sent him to Bavaria, where he became abbot of Saint Peter's in Salzburg.
beats.scene: Tonsured monks in simple habits greet a newly arrived abbot at the gate of a modest stone abbey beneath the Alpine hills above Salzburg.

beats.text: A priest once baptized with faulty Latin. Boniface complained to the pope. Virgil held it valid, and Pope Zachary agreed.
beats.scene: In a small early medieval Bavarian church, a priest pours water over an infant at a stone font while Virgil, in monastic dress, watches calmly with one hand raised.

beats.text: On the other charge, the pope ordered a council only if it was proved. Virgil cleared himself.
beats.scene: Pope Zachary sits on a plain throne in an eighth-century Roman hall, in papal vestments, dictating a letter to a scribe. Scrolls lie on the table between them.

beats.text: As bishop, he built Salzburg's cathedral, and sent missionaries to the people of Carinthia.
beats.scene: Virgil stands in bishop's vestments with his crozier, overseeing masons raising the walls of a stone cathedral in Salzburg. In the background, monks set out along a mountain road toward the Alpine valleys.

beats.text: He stayed, and served where he was sent. Saint Virgil, pray for us.

claims.claim: Virgil was an Irish monk and priest of the eighth century
He left Ireland around 745 meaning to visit the Holy Land but settled in Francia
Pippin received him with great favour
Pippin sent him on to Bavaria, where he became abbot of Saint Peter's in Salzburg
A priest, through ignorance, baptized with an incorrect Latin formula; Virgil held the baptism valid; Boniface complained to Pope Zachary, who decided in Virgil's favour
Boniface accused Virgil of teaching about other people beneath the earth, contrary to Scripture
Pope Zachary ruled that a council should be held only if it were clearly established that Virgil held this belief
Virgil succeeded in freeing himself from the charge of teaching a doctrine contrary to Scripture
He built Salzburg's cathedral, consecrated in 774, in honour of Saint Rupert
He sent missionaries to the Carantanians (Carinthia)
Modestus was sent in 755 at the request of Duke Boruth to Maria Saal near Klagenfurt, from where Christianity spread in Carinthia
He was canonized by Pope Gregory IX in 1233, on 18 June
He died in Salzburg on 27 November 784
His grave was forgotten soon after his death, rediscovered in 1181, and his bones moved to a new tomb in 1288
He is patron of Salzburg, of children and of childbirth
At his death 67 churches depended on Salzburg as proprietary churches
The Tassilo Chalice, perhaps the oldest chalice in the world, was made in his time
Identification with Fergil, abbot of Aghaboe, is possible but unproven; his exact birth date is uncertain

story: Virgil came from Ireland, which the people of his age called Hibernia. That much is among the best-founded facts of his life. Almost everything else about his beginnings is uncertain: the place and date of his birth, his family, even the monastery where he was formed. The usual date of around 700 is an estimate, not a recorded fact. Some sources suggest a link to a noble Irish family and to the monastery of Iona, but these are clues, not proof. Many writers have also identified him with Fergil, abbot of Aghaboe in what is now County Laois. Careful modern reference works call that identification possible but not proven.

What is clear is the world that shaped him. Irish monasteries of the eighth century were lively places of learning, with schools of Scripture, grammar and the calculation of the calendar, and with a great love of Latin books. Like many of his countrymen, Virgil set out from home as a pilgrim for Christ. He left Ireland around the middle of the 740s, meaning to visit the Holy Land. He never got there. He settled instead among the Franks, where Pippin, who was not yet king, received him with great favour and kept him at court for about two years.

Pippin then sent him on to Bavaria, to Duke Odilo. At Salzburg, Virgil became abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter. Salzburg already had a Christian past, tied to Saint Rupert, and it lay on the roads between Bavaria, the Alpine valleys and the Slavic lands. The Church there was a tangle of monasteries, ducal power and the rights of bishops. Historians still debate the exact order of his abbacy and his consecration as bishop. Older accounts place his consecration in 766 or 767, while more recent studies suggest about 749.

These early years brought him into conflict with Saint Boniface, the great missionary and papal legate in Germany. The first dispute concerned a priest who, through ignorance of Latin, had baptized with an incorrect formula. Virgil held that the baptism was valid. Boniface complained to Pope Zachary, and the pope decided in Virgil's favour.

The second dispute is the one that made Virgil famous. Boniface accused him of teaching about other people beneath the earth, which he called contrary to Scripture. The pope answered with caution. If it were clearly established that Virgil held such a belief, a council should be called. Virgil's own treatise has been lost, so we cannot read his argument. We do know that he cleared himself of the charge. It is likely that Boniface feared that people on the far side of the world could not be descendants of Adam or redeemed by Christ. Virgil, no doubt, could show that his teaching meant nothing of the kind. It is thought that his belief in the antipodes came from ancient geographers and from the accounts of Irish voyagers. He is also known as "the Geometer."

Whatever was said of his ideas, his work was plain to see. He built a cathedral in Salzburg, in honour of Saint Rupert, and it was consecrated in 774. He also had Rupert's relics placed in its crypt. He strengthened the Church's property and institutions, and 67 churches depended on Salzburg when he died. In 755, at the request of the Slavic duke Boruth, he sent his companion Modestus to Maria Saal, near Klagenfurt. From there Christianity spread through Carinthia, and Virgil came to be called its apostle. The arts flourished in his time as well. The Tassilo Chalice, perhaps the oldest chalice in the world, was made then.

Virgil died in Salzburg on 27 November 784. One older reference gives 789, but most references give 784. His grave was soon forgotten. It was found again in 1181 during rebuilding of the cathedral, and in 1288 his bones were moved to a new tomb. Pope Gregory IX canonized him on 18 June 1233. He is patron of Salzburg and its diocese, and of children and of childbirth. A statue of him stands outside the cathedral doors. He is remembered as a scholar and a builder, an Irish pilgrim who stayed and served where he was sent.

es.name: San Virgilio de Salzburgo
es.hook: Un monje irlandés, una tierra redonda y una carta enviada a Roma.
es.summary: San Virgilio de Salzburgo, monje irlandés, fue denunciado ante el papa por sus ideas sobre el mundo, se justificó y después construyó la catedral de Salzburgo y envió misioneros a Carintia.
story: Virgilio procedía de Irlanda, a la que los pueblos de su tiempo llamaban Hibernia. Ese dato se cuenta entre los mejor documentados de su vida. Casi todo lo demás sobre sus inicios es incierto: el lugar y la fecha de su nacimiento, su familia e incluso el monasterio en el que se formó. La fecha habitual de alrededor del año 700 es una estimación, no un hecho registrado. Algunas fuentes sugieren un vínculo con una noble familia irlandesa y con el monasterio de Iona, pero se trata de indicios, no de pruebas. Muchos autores también lo han identificado con Fergil, abad de Aghaboe, en lo que hoy es el condado de Laois. Las obras de referencia modernas y rigurosas consideran posible esa identificación, pero no demostrada.

Lo que sí está claro es el mundo que lo formó. Los monasterios irlandeses del siglo VIII eran centros vivos de saber, con escuelas de Escritura, gramática y cálculo del calendario, y con un gran amor por los libros en latín. Como muchos de sus compatriotas, Virgilio salió de su tierra como peregrino por Cristo. Abandonó Irlanda hacia mediados de los años 740, con la intención de visitar Tierra Santa. Nunca llegó allí. En cambio, se estableció entre los francos, donde Pipino, que todavía no era rey, lo recibió con gran benevolencia y lo mantuvo en la corte durante unos dos años.

Después, Pipino lo envió a Baviera, junto al duque Odilón. En Salzburgo, Virgilio llegó a ser abad del monasterio de San Pedro. Salzburgo ya tenía un pasado cristiano, ligado a San Ruperto, y se encontraba en los caminos entre Baviera, los valles alpinos y las tierras eslavas. La Iglesia de la zona era una maraña de monasterios, poder ducal y derechos episcopales. Los historiadores todavía debaten el orden exacto de su abadiato y de su consagración como obispo. Las relaciones más antiguas sitúan su consagración en 766 o 767, mientras que estudios más recientes sugieren hacia el año 749.

Estos primeros años lo llevaron a un conflicto con San Bonifacio, gran misionero y legado papal en Germania. La primera disputa se refería a un sacerdote que, por ignorancia del latín, había bautizado con una fórmula incorrecta. Virgilio sostenía que el bautismo era válido. Bonifacio se quejó al papa Zacarías, y el papa resolvió a favor de Virgilio.

La segunda disputa es la que hizo famoso a Virgilio. Bonifacio lo acusó de enseñar la existencia de otros seres humanos bajo la tierra, lo que consideró contrario a la Escritura. El papa respondió con cautela: si se establecía con claridad que Virgilio sostenía tal creencia, debía convocarse un concilio. El tratado propio de Virgilio se ha perdido, por lo que no podemos leer su argumentación. Sí sabemos que se justificó de la acusación. Es probable que Bonifacio temiera que las personas situadas al otro lado del mundo no pudieran descender de Adán ni ser redimidas por Cristo. Virgilio, sin duda, pudo demostrar que su enseñanza no significaba nada de eso. Se piensa que su creencia en los antípodas procedía de antiguos geógrafos y de los relatos de navegantes irlandeses. También es conocido como «el Geómetra».

Fuera lo que fuera lo que se dijo de sus ideas, su obra era evidente. Construyó una catedral en Salzburgo, en honor de San Ruperto, que fue consagrada en 774. Además, hizo colocar las reliquias de Ruperto en su cripta. Fortaleció los bienes e instituciones de la Iglesia, y al morir dependían de Salzburgo 67 iglesias. En 755, a petición del duque eslavo Boruth, envió a su compañero Modesto a Maria Saal, cerca de Klagenfurt. Desde allí el cristianismo se extendió por Carintia, y Virgilio llegó a ser llamado su apóstol. Las artes también florecieron en su época. En aquel tiempo se hizo el Cáliz de Tasilón, quizá el cáliz más antiguo del mundo.

Virgilio murió en Salzburgo el 27 de noviembre de 784. Una obra de referencia antigua da el año 789, pero la mayoría da 784. Su sepultura pronto cayó en el olvido. Fue hallada de nuevo en 1181, durante la reconstrucción de la catedral, y en 1288 sus restos fueron trasladados a una tumba nueva. El papa Gregorio IX lo canonizó el 18 de junio de 1233. Es patrón de Salzburgo y de su diócesis, así como de los niños y del parto. Una estatua suya se alza fuera de las puertas de la catedral. Se le recuerda como erudito y constructor, un peregrino irlandés que se quedó y sirvió allí donde fue enviado.
es.prayer: Se quedó, y sirvió allí donde fue enviado. San Virgilio, ruega por nosotros.
